findings.title: Denial-cache test would pass without the denial cache
findings.body: The comment says this cache entry grants access "to prove this is not checked", but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. `checkPermission` only allows on a truthy value (`scopeMap[t.scope(req.Name)]`, service.go:558), so this entry denies. The DB fallback then uses the empty `fakeStore` from `setupService` (service_test.go:1328) and denies too. If you removed the `permDenialCache` short-circuit (service.go:116-121), `resp.Allowed` would still be false, so the test never exercises the code it is named after. Set the value to `true`, or point the store at a permission that grants dash1, so the test fails without the denial-cache check.

findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous when names contain `_`
findings.body: `name` and `parent` are joined with `_`, and resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores. So `name="a", parent="b_c"` and `name="a_b", parent="c"` both produce `..._a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource can then deny a different resource for up to `shortCacheTTL` (30s), and nothing logs it. The collision can only cause false denials, never false grants. A separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or length-prefixing the parts, would remove the ambiguity.

findings.title: Denial cache undoes the new fallback-on-cached-deny for repeated checks
findings.body: The new Check flow goes to the DB when the cached permissions deny (service.go:123-139), so a freshly granted permission is seen right away (the "Fallback to the database on outdated cache" test). After the first denial, though, `permDenialCache` is set for `shortCacheTTL` (30s, service.go:32). Every later check for the same user, action, name and folder then short-circuits to deny at service.go:117 without looking at the permission cache or the DB. A user who was just granted access and retries keeps getting denied for up to 30s. That is about the same staleness as before the change, so this is not a regression, but the asymmetry is worth deciding on deliberately. For example, a shorter TTL for denials, or a comment explaining the trade-off.

findings.title: `cacheHit` field and its branches are now dead
findings.body: The only case with `cacheHit: true` was removed, and `getUserPermissions` no longer reads the permission cache. So `cacheHit` is always false, and the branches at lines 367-369 and 388-390 never run. Remove the field and those branches.

contracts.action: Check consults permDenialCache, then cached permissions, before falling back to the DB
contracts.before_after: Before: a permCache hit was final, whether it allowed or denied. After: a cached allow is final; a cached deny falls back to the DB; a DB deny writes a denial entry for 30s.
contracts.visible_effect: Access grants are visible right away the first time; repeated denied checks are served from the denial cache for up to 30s.
contracts.failure_mode: GetUserIdentifiers error in getCachedIdentityPermissions falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which retries and returns the error (deny).

contracts.action: List uses cached permissions when present, otherwise the DB
contracts.equivalent_path: getIdentityPermissions previously checked the cache internally
contracts.before_after: Same behavior; cache lookup moved up into List.
contracts.visible_effect: Same list results; metrics now emitted in List.
contracts.failure_mode: Cache error falls back to the DB; a DB error is returned as before.

contracts.action: In-process authz client uses NoopCache instead of a 30s local cache
contracts.before_after: Before: client-side results cached for 30s in-process. After: every in-process check reaches the server, which has its own caches.
contracts.failure_mode: NoopCache always misses, so nothing is cached client-side.

summary: The PR moves the RBAC service's permission-cache reads into Check and List. A cached deny now falls back to the DB, and a new 30s denial cache records DB denials. The in-process client cache becomes a no-op. The main defect is in a test: the denial-cache test would pass without the denial cache. There are also three judgement calls: the denial cache key can be ambiguous, the denial cache undoes the immediate-grant fallback for repeated checks, and a test field is now dead.
